title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Stars Went Missing
moral: When you feel lost, helping someone else find their way will light the path for both of you.

pages.content:
The Silverbell Forest was not a place you found. It was a place that found you, slipping into the space between a yawn and sleep, arriving like a word you'd been trying to remember all day.

{{NAME}} stepped between two enormous white birch trees and breathed in a scent like cold rivers and summer flowers and something else entirely, something that had no name but felt like happiness remembered. The forest floor glittered faintly, as though scattered with invisible diamonds.

Above him, the sky was wrong. Not frightening, just wrong in a very precise way. It was perfectly black. Not the warm, star-dusted black of a good night sky, but the flat, empty black of a chalkboard wiped clean. Not a single star burned overhead.

A sound came from ahead. Something between a bell and a sob. {{NAME}} followed it deeper into the silver trees, his trainers crunching softly on the glittering ground, until the trees parted and he found himself in a clearing full of fairies and one very unhappy unicorn.

pages.content:
The unicorn was smaller than {{NAME}} had expected, about the size of a large dog, with a coat the colour of fresh snow and a mane that should have been shimmering silver but was currently the grey-brown of an overcast morning. Her horn, which ought to have glowed, was entirely dark.

Her name was Lumen, and she was the Keeper of Stars.

A tiny fairy named Thistle, sharp-eyed and quick-fingered, explained the situation with great urgency from her seat on Lumen's nose. Each night, Lumen walked the Sky Path, the invisible bridge from the forest's highest peak to the edge of the horizon, and as she walked, stars lit in her hoofprints. But tonight Lumen had lost her way. She'd taken a wrong path in the daytime and now couldn't remember the beginning of the Sky Path, and without the first step, the whole route was dark.

Lumen's deep violet eyes found {{NAME}}'s face. "I've been trying to remember for hours," she said, in a voice like a struck crystal glass. "I'm afraid the night will never have stars again."

pages.content:
{{NAME}} thought carefully. He didn't know the Sky Path. But he did know something about finding things when you couldn't remember where you left them.

"Tell me what you noticed today," he said to Lumen. "Before you got lost. What did you see? What did you hear?"

Lumen blinked. It wasn't the question she'd expected. She thought. "A river," she said slowly. "Running west. And a field of blue clover. And a stone shaped like a sleeping owl."

Thistle snapped her fingers. "The owl-stone is three fields east of the peak! I know it!" She launched from Lumen's nose like a small arrow. "Follow me!"

They moved through the forest together, the four of them, because two more fairies had appeared, Briar and Wren, drawn by the commotion. Briar lit their path with a lantern-glow. Wren sang softly, a song that seemed to help Lumen remember each next step. And {{NAME}} kept asking questions, gentle questions, patient questions, the kind that unlocked doors inside a memory.

When they reached the owl-stone, Lumen stopped. Lifted her head. And took one slow, certain step forward onto a path only she could feel.

pages.content:
The Sky Path opened before Lumen like a road made of held breath. Each hoofprint she placed blazed white-gold, and from each one a star rose, drifting upward in a slow, stately spiral to take its place in the dark sky above.

One. Ten. Fifty. A hundred.

The fairies watched from the highest branch of the tallest tree, silent for once, their faces tipped upward, bathed in the returning starlight. Thistle had both hands pressed to her cheeks. Briar's lantern had gone out, because it was no longer needed.

It was one of the most beautiful things {{NAME}} had ever seen. But the most beautiful moment was smaller. It was when Lumen paused mid-path and looked back at him from the sky. Her horn blazed like a lighthouse. Her mane was silver again, truly silver, flowing in a wind that came from nowhere. She didn't say anything. She didn't have to.

{{NAME}} watched every star find its place, his neck craned back, eyes wide, the cold night air cool on his upturned face. The sky filled and filled and filled.

pages.content:
The sky, when Lumen had finished, was the richest, most crowded, most extravagantly beautiful sky {{NAME}} had ever seen. Stars pressed against each other, jostling for space, each one singing its own tiny light.

Thistle presented {{NAME}} with a single star-seed, no bigger than a grain of rice, which she pressed into his palm with both hands. "Plant it in soil," she said firmly. "Water it once. See what grows."

The birch trees opened as they always did, without fuss, and {{NAME}} walked home through the newly starred night, the seed warm in his closed fist. He placed it in the small pot of soil on his windowsill before he climbed into bed, pressed it deep with one careful finger.

The night was full of stars above him, and their light was soft on his ceiling as his eyes grew heavy. He fell asleep watching the light move, slow and peaceful, across the wall.

In the morning, {{NAME}} was the first one awake. He padded to the windowsill in his socks, and there, in the pot, pushing bravely through the soil, was a single small shoot, and at its very tip, the faintest silver glow.
